Georg Spalatin
gā´ōrk spä´la-tēn
n. (Georg Spalatin, 1484–1545, secretary and chaplain to Frederick the Wise, the courtier through whom Luther was protected and the Elector persuaded)
Latinized from Burkhardt of Spalt in Franconia — Spalatinus, of Spalt; Georg, from Greek georgos, a husbandman.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Georg Spalatin never wrote a book of doctrine and is one of the three or four men without whom there would have been no Reformation. As private secretary, chaplain and librarian to Frederick the Wise of Saxony, he had the ear of the one prince able to shield Luther from the empire, and he used it continuously for twenty years: translating Luther's Latin for the Elector, interpreting the Elector's mind to Luther, drafting the refusal to surrender him after Exsurge Domine, and arranging the kidnapping that hid him in the Wartburg after Worms. He was cautious where Luther was bold and often restrained him, sometimes rightly. His office is Nehemiah's. “Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven” (Neh 2:4) is the courtier's moment, and Neh 1:11 the prayer before it: “grant him mercy in the sight of this man.” Dan 1:9 names who gives such favour: “Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs.” Pro 16:7 is the providence of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines favor as kind regard; kindness; countenance; propitious aspect; friendly disposition; and a courtier as one who attends or frequents the courts of princes.

expand to see more

FA'VOR, n. Kind regard; kindness; countenance; propitious aspect; friendly disposition.

2. Support; defense; vindication; or disposition to aid, befriend, support, promote or justify.

COUR'TIER, n. One who attends or frequents the courts of princes.

Key Scripture

Neh 2:4 — "Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven."

Neh 1:11 — "O Lord, I beseech thee, let now thine ear be attentive to the prayer of thy servant, and to the prayer of thy servants, who desire to fear thy name: and prosper, I pray thee, thy servant this day, and grant him mercy in the sight of this man. For I was the king's cupbearer."

Dan 1:9 — "Now God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs."

Pro 16:7 — "When a man's ways please the LORD, he maketh even his enemies to be at peace with him."

Modern Corruption

God protected the Reformation through a civil servant, and a church that only recognizes pulpit callings cannot see what He was doing.

expand to see more

Spalatin held no office in the church and spent his working life drafting letters for a prince, and the gospel in Germany survived because he was where he was. Scripture is full of the pattern — Joseph in the prison and then the palace, Daniel with the prince of the eunuchs, Nehemiah with the cup, Esther with access, Erastus the chamberlain — and in every case the favour is traced to God, not to the courtier's skill. Dan 1:9 is explicit about the agent. A doctrine of vocation that ranks the secretary beneath the preacher has not read these accounts carefully.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the lawful use of access, together with its limit. Spalatin's caution more than once nearly smothered the thing he was protecting, and he advised Luther to be quiet at moments when silence would have been surrender; the courtier's temptation is to make prudence the highest virtue. Neh 2:4 holds the balance exactly — the request is made to the king, and it is made by a man who prayed first to the God of heaven, which is what keeps access from becoming mere management.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chesed (H2617), mercy, lovingkindness; racham (H7356), tender love; ratsah (H7521), to be pleased with.

Hebrew baqqashah (H1246) — a request, a petition; Nehemiah 2:4.

Hebrew rachamim (H7356) — mercies, tender love; Nehemiah 1:11, Daniel 1:9.

Hebrew chesed (H2617) — mercy, steadfast love; Daniel 1:9.

Hebrew ratsah (H7521) — to be pleased with, to accept; Proverbs 16:7.

Usage

"“So I prayed to the God of heaven” (Neh 2:4) — the courtier's moment."

"“grant him mercy in the sight of this man” (Neh 1:11) — the prayer behind the access."

"“God had brought Daniel into favour and tender love with the prince of the eunuchs” (Dan 1:9) — who gives such favour."
